questions.question: Which of the following is the easternmost international border point of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kibithu**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Kibithu** is located in the Anjaw district of Arunachal Pradesh, India, and is the easternmost inhabited village near the international border with China.
 
• It is strategically significant as it lies at the tri-junction of India, China, and Myanmar, making it vital for border security and trade.
 
• Kibithu is situated at an altitude of approximately 4,070 feet above sea level, offering stunning views of the Lohit River valley.
 
• This area was a crucial point of engagement during the 1962 Sino-Indian War, and it continues to be a region of strategic importance for India’s defense forces.
 
• Due to its geographical location, Kibithu plays a critical role in monitoring and maintaining the integrity of India’s eastern borders.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Nathu La:**

 
 
• Located in Sikkim, Nathu La is a mountain pass on the Indo-China border, crucial for trade and military operations.
 
• It connects India’s Sikkim state with China’s Tibet Autonomous Region.
 
 
 
• **Lipulekh:**
 
 
• Located in Uttarakhand, Lipulekh Pass serves as a gateway to Kailash Mansarovar in Tibet.
 
• The pass is part of the disputed Kalapani region claimed by both India and Nepal.
 
 
 
• **Rohtang:**
 
 
• Rohtang Pass is situated in Himachal Pradesh, connecting Kullu Valley with Lahaul and Spiti Valley.
 
• It is not located near India’s international borders.
 
 
 
• **India's Easternmost Point:**
 
 
• The easternmost point of India is not Kibithu but the disputed territory of Vijaynagar in Arunachal Pradesh.
 
• Kibithu is the easternmost international border settlement in India.

questions.question: Morarji Desai was commemorated on his 129th birth anniversary, 28 February 2025, for his contributions to governance reforms in India. Which of the following commissions did he chair in 1966 to restructure the country’s governance?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1st Administrative Reforms Commission**__.

__
 
• The **1st Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC)** was established in 1966 under the chairmanship of **Morarji Desai** to review and recommend changes to the administrative structure of India.
 
• The Commission submitted its reports over the next few years, covering various aspects of administration such as personnel management, financial administration, and center-state relations.
 
• It focused on **reforms in governance** to make the Indian administrative system more efficient, transparent, and responsive to the needs of citizens.
 
• The 1st ARC produced **20 detailed reports**, which included over 500 actionable recommendations.
 
• Some of the key areas addressed included **administrative accountability, ethics in governance, and citizen-centric services.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC)**:

 
 
• The ARC is constituted by the government to examine the state of public administration and suggest reforms.
 
• The recommendations of the 1st ARC laid the foundation for modern governance reforms in India.
 
• Its reports covered areas such as local governance, interdepartmental coordination, and the role of public sector enterprises.
 
 
 
• **Morarji Desai**:
 
 
• He was the 4th Prime Minister of India and served from 1977 to 1979.
 
• Desai was known for his integrity, administrative skills, and commitment to governance reforms.
 
• He played a vital role in shaping India's administrative policies during his tenure as a public servant and leader.
 
 
 
• **Key Impact of the 1st ARC**:
 
 
• The reports influenced the creation of institutions such as the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) and reforms in personnel management.
 
• It emphasized the importance of ethics, accountability, and citizen participation in governance.
 
 
 
• **Subsequent ARCs**:
 
 
• The 2nd Administrative Reforms Commission (2005-2009) built upon the recommendations of the 1st ARC.
 
• It focused on improving governance in areas such as disaster management, e-governance, and local self-governance.

questions.question: Which Fundamental Right was subjected to additional restrictions by the First Amendment Act of 1951?

options.text: Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The First Amendment Act of 1951 brought additional restrictions to the **Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression** under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India.
 
• It introduced provisions allowing the state to impose "reasonable restrictions" on this right in the interests of **public order, security, decency, morality, sovereignty, and integrity of India.**
 
• The amendment was enacted to address issues arising from judicial interpretations that had invalidated several laws restricting speech and expression.
 
• The Act also added Article 19(2), which explicitly states the grounds on which the government can limit the right to freedom of speech and expression.
 
• This amendment was a response to decisions like the Romesh Thapar vs State of Madras case, where the Supreme Court struck down laws restricting press freedom.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights in India:**

 
 
• Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution and are considered essential for individual freedom and democracy.
 
• They include rights such as equality, freedom, protection against exploitation, freedom of religion, and constitutional remedies.
 
• These rights are enforceable by the judiciary and can be challenged in a court of law.
 
 
 
• **Article 19(1) of the Indian Constitution:**
 
 
• Article 19(1) guarantees six freedoms to citizens, including the right to freedom of speech and expression.
 
• These freedoms are subject to reasonable restrictions for maintaining public order, morality, and sovereignty.
 
 
 
• **Romesh Thapar vs State of Madras (1950):**
 
 
• This landmark case challenged restrictions imposed on the press under public order laws.
 
• The Supreme Court invalidated these laws, prompting the government to introduce the First Amendment Act.
 
 
 
• **Reasonable Restrictions:**
 
 
• The First Amendment introduced the concept of "reasonable restrictions" to ensure a balance between individual freedom and societal interests.
 
• Grounds for restriction include security, sovereignty, morality, and public order.

questions.question: After the revolt of which year did the British implement measures that reduced the proportion of Indian soldiers in the army and increased the number of European soldiers?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1857**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The revolt of 1857, also known as the First War of Independence or Sepoy Mutiny, led to significant changes in British military policies in India.
 
• Post-1857, the proportion of Indian soldiers in the army was systematically reduced while the number of European soldiers increased significantly to prevent future rebellions.
 
• The British reorganized the Indian Army by increasing the ratio of European to Indian soldiers from 1:6 to 1:2 in critical areas.
 
• Key changes included stricter recruitment policies, favoring soldiers from certain regions and communities such as Punjabis and Gurkhas, who were considered more loyal.
 
• The British also positioned European troops in strategically important locations and ensured their control over key artillery units.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Revolt of 1857:**

 
 
• It was triggered by multiple factors, including resentment against British policies, economic exploitation, and the introduction of the Enfield rifle cartridges rumored to be greased with cow and pig fat.
 
• The revolt began in Meerut and quickly spread across northern and central India, involving soldiers, peasants, and local rulers.
 
• Prominent leaders included Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, Tantia Tope, Nana Sahib, and Begum Hazrat Mahal.
 
 
 
• **British Military Reforms Post-1857:**
 
 
• The command structure of the army was centralized under British control.
 
• Significant investments were made in infrastructure, such as railways and telegraphs, to enable rapid troop movement.
 
• European officers were placed in key positions, and Indian soldiers were deliberately kept away from sensitive areas like artillery.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Revolt:**
 
 
• The revolt led to the end of the East India Company's rule, and governance was transferred directly to the British Crown under the Government of India Act 1858.
 
• It also marked a shift in British policies, with a focus on consolidating power and preventing further uprisings.
 
 
 
• **Terminology:**
 
 
• "Sepoy Mutiny" is a term used by British historians, while Indian historians often refer to it as the "First War of Independence."
 
• The term "divide and rule" was implemented more rigorously post-1857 to maintain control by exploiting religious and regional divisions.

questions.question: Which uprising in Uttar Pradesh, led by Mufti Muhammad Aiwaz, was among the most significant revolts against British rule in India prior to the First War of Independence in 1857?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bareilly Uprisings**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Bareilly Uprisings were an important revolt against British rule in India, occurring in the early 19th century, prior to the First War of Independence in 1857.
 
• These uprisings were led by Mufti Muhammad Aiwaz, who played a critical role in mobilizing resistance against British colonial policies.
 
• The revolt primarily took place in the Bareilly region of present-day Uttar Pradesh and reflected the growing unrest among Indian communities under British rule.
 
• The uprising was driven by widespread dissatisfaction with British economic exploitation, religious interference, and administrative policies.
 
• The Bareilly Uprisings are considered significant precursors to the larger and more organized rebellions that culminated in the Revolt of 1857.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Revolt of 1857:**

 
 
• The Revolt of 1857, also known as India's First War of Independence, marked a significant uprising against British rule in India.
 
• It was sparked by a combination of political, economic, social, and military grievances, including the introduction of the Enfield rifle cartridge rumored to be greased with cow and pig fat.
 
• The revolt was led by various leaders across regions, including Rani Lakshmibai, Tantia Tope, Bahadur Shah Zafar, and Nana Saheb.
 
• The uprising was ultimately suppressed by the British, but it marked a turning point in India's struggle for independence.
 
 
 
• **Other Regional Uprisings Pre-1857:**
 
 
• **Kol Uprisings:** Tribal rebellion in the Chotanagpur region (1831-1832) against British exploitation and land revenue policies.
 
• **Santhal Rebellion:** A tribal revolt in 1855-1856 in present-day Jharkhand, led by Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu, against oppressive landlords and British policies.
 
• **Chuar Rebellion:** A series of uprisings in Bengal and Bihar during the late 18th century by tribal communities resisting British revenue collection.
 
 
 
• **Mufti Muhammad Aiwaz:**
 
 
• Mufti Muhammad Aiwaz was a prominent leader of the Bareilly Uprisings and played a crucial role in uniting people against British authority.
 
• He symbolized resistance to British interference in the religious and social practices of Indian communities.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Early Uprisings:**
 
 
• These early uprisings highlighted the growing resentment among Indians toward British policies and exploitation.
 
• They laid the foundation for organized resistance movements in the 19th and 20th centuries, culminating in India's independence in 1947.

questions.question: What natural feature existed between the Himalayas and the Deccan Plateau before the formation of the Great Plain?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A shallow trough or geosyncline**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Indo-Gangetic Plain, also called the Great Plain, was formed due to the gradual filling of a **shallow trough or geosyncline** that existed between the Himalayas and the Deccan Plateau.
 
• This geosyncline, known as the **Tethys Sea**, was a depression that existed millions of years ago during the Mesozoic era.
 
• Over time, sediments from the rising Himalayas and other sources filled this trough, leading to the formation of the vast alluvial plains of Northern India.
 
• The process of sedimentation was facilitated by rivers like the Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra, which transported eroded material from the mountains to the plains.
 
• The Great Plain is now one of the most fertile regions in the world, supporting agriculture and a dense population.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Geosyncline:**

 
 
• A geosyncline is a large-scale depression in the Earth's crust filled with thick layers of sediments.
 
• It often forms in areas where two tectonic plates converge, leading to subsidence and sediment accumulation.
 
• Over geological time, geosynclines may become mountain ranges or plains due to tectonic uplift and erosion.
 
 
 
• **Tethys Sea:**
 
 
• The Tethys Sea was a prehistoric ocean that existed between the ancient continents of Laurasia (to the north) and Gondwana (to the south).
 
• It played a key role in the tectonic evolution of Asia, Europe, and the Indian subcontinent.
 
• Its closure due to the collision of the Indian Plate with the Eurasian Plate led to the uplift of the Himalayas.
 
 
 
• **Himalayan Sedimentation:**
 
 
• The Himalayas are the primary source of sediments that filled the Indo-Gangetic trough.
 
• Rivers originating from the Himalayas carry eroded materials and deposit them in the plains.
 
• This sedimentation process has been ongoing for millions of years, shaping the fertile plains.
 
 
 
• **Indo-Gangetic Plain:**
 
 
• One of the world's largest alluvial plains, extending over 7 lakh square kilometers across India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh.
 
• It is drained by major rivers, including the Ganga, Yamuna, Brahmaputra, and their tributaries.
 
• The plain is known for its rich soil, which supports intensive agriculture and sustains a high population density.

• Behramji Merwanji Malabari's **'The Indian Muse in English Garb'** is a collection of poems published in 1876.
 
• The book comprises a total of **32 poems**, showcasing the blending of Indian themes with English literary styles.
 
• Malabari was a notable Indian poet and social reformer, known for his advocacy against child marriage and for women's rights.
 
• The poems in the collection reflect themes of patriotism, spirituality, and social issues relevant to Indian society during the colonial era.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Behramji Malabari**:

 
 
• Born in 1853 in Baroda, Malabari was a prominent Indian poet, writer, and social reformer.
 
• He is best known for his efforts to abolish **child marriage** and improve the status of women in India.
 
• His writings combined progressive social ideas with literary creativity.
 
 
 
• **Indian Literature in English**:

• Works such as 'The Indian Muse in English Garb' showcased Indian themes rendered in English literary tradition.

• **Colonial Influence on Indian Writing**:

• **Social Reform in 19th Century India**:

• Literature often served as a vehicle for promoting these reformist ideas.

questions.question: What was India’s external debt to GDP ratio at the end of September 2024?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**0.194**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• India's external debt to GDP ratio at the end of September 2024 was **19.4% (0.194)**, indicating a moderate level of external debt relative to its GDP.
 
• This ratio is a critical indicator of a country’s ability to manage and repay its external debt obligations efficiently.
 
• A lower external debt-to-GDP ratio is generally considered favorable as it reflects a lower debt burden in comparison to the country’s economic output.
 
• India has consistently maintained a sustainable external debt level, supported by its strong foreign exchange reserves.
 
• The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) periodically monitors and publishes data on the country's external debt to ensure transparency and economic stability.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **External Debt:**

 
 
• External debt refers to the total borrowing by a country from foreign lenders, including governments, financial institutions, and private entities.
 
• It typically includes loans, bonds, and other financial instruments owed to non-residents.
 
 
 
• **External Debt to GDP Ratio:**
 
 
• This ratio is calculated by dividing a country’s total external debt by its Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
 
• A lower ratio indicates that the country’s economic output is sufficient to cover its debt obligations, reducing the risk of default.
 
 
 
• **India’s External Debt Composition:**
 
 
• India’s external debt is categorized into short-term and long-term debt, with long-term debt constituting a significant share.
 
• Major components include commercial borrowings, NRI deposits, and multilateral loans.
 
 
 
• **Role of Foreign Exchange Reserves:**
 
 
• India’s foreign exchange reserves act as a buffer to manage external debt obligations and ensure economic stability.
 
• As of recent years, India has maintained substantial reserves to meet its debt servicing requirements comfortably.

questions.question: Overall, the Panchayati Raj system in India is designed to promote:

options.text: economic austerity across the country for people's betterment
central control over local areas across the country
democratic governance and empowerment at the grassroots level
international funding for local projects, ensuring adequate development

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**democratic governance and empowerment at the grassroots level**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Panchayati Raj system in India was introduced to ensure **decentralized governance** and empower local bodies.
 
• It was formally established through the **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992**, which added Part IX to the Constitution.
 
• The system provides a platform for **grassroots democracy** by enabling local self-government in rural areas.
 
• It aims to empower villagers by involving them in **decision-making processes** and ensuring effective implementation of developmental programs.
 
• Key principles include **decentralization, transparency, and accountability** to promote inclusive development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992**

 
 
• This act provided a constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions.
 
• It mandated the creation of a three-tier system: **Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, and Zilla Parishad**.
 
• It introduced the concept of **reservations for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and women** in Panchayati Raj institutions.
 
• Article 243A allows the Gram Sabha to function as the foundation of grassroots democracy.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of Panchayati Raj**
 
 
• Regular elections every 5 years to ensure accountability.
 
• State governments are required to establish a **State Election Commission** to oversee these elections.
 
• State Finance Commissions are constituted to recommend the allocation of financial resources to Panchayats.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Grassroots Democracy**
 
 
• Empowers local communities by allowing them to identify their needs and priorities.
 
• Promotes **social inclusion** by involving marginalized sections in governance.
 
• Enhances governance efficiency by addressing issues at the local level.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Implementation**
 
 
• Lack of financial autonomy and dependency on state governments.
 
• Inadequate capacity building and training for elected representatives.
 
• Uneven development due to socio-economic disparities in rural areas.

questions.question: With reference to computing, what does ASCII stand for?

options.text: Algorithmic Standard Code for International Information
American Standard Code for Information Integrity
American Standard Code for Information Interchange
American Systematic Code for International Interoperability

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**American Standard Code for Information Interchange**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **ASCII** stands for **American Standard Code for Information Interchange**, a character encoding standard for electronic communication.
 
• It was first published in **1963** by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) as a standardized way to represent text in computers.
 
• ASCII uses **7-bit binary numbers** to represent 128 different characters, including letters, digits, punctuation marks, and control characters.
 
• It is widely used in **computers, communication devices, and other electronic systems** to represent text data.
 
• The extended ASCII version (8-bit) includes an additional 128 characters, making it compatible with more languages and symbols.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Control Characters:**

 
 
• ASCII includes control characters like **carriage return (CR)**, **line feed (LF)**, and **tab**, which are used for text formatting and communication control.
 
• These characters do not represent printable symbols but perform specific functions in data transmission and processing.
 
 
 
• **Unicode:**
 
 
• Unicode is a more modern character encoding standard that extends ASCII, allowing representation of characters from virtually all languages and symbols.
 
• While ASCII uses 7 bits, Unicode can use up to 32 bits for encoding, making it more versatile for global applications.
 
 
 
• **Binary Representation:**
 
 
• Each ASCII character is represented by a unique binary code, such as **01000001** for the letter 'A'.
 
• This binary representation ensures compatibility with digital systems.
 
 
 
• **Applications of ASCII:**
 
 
• ASCII is used in programming, file formats, and data storage to ensure consistency in text representation.
 
• It is the basis for text encoding in protocols like **HTTP, SMTP, and FTP**.

questions.question: The President's power to seek the Supreme Court's opinion on questions of law comes under ___________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 143**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 143 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to seek the opinion of the Supreme Court on questions of law or fact that are of public importance.
 
• The advice provided by the Supreme Court under Article 143 is not binding on the President; it is advisory in nature.
 
• This provision is often referred to as the "Advisory Jurisdiction" of the Supreme Court.
 
• Article 143 is invoked to resolve complex legal or constitutional matters that require judicial interpretation.
 
• The President can exercise this power either on his own discretion or based on advice from the Council of Ministers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Advisory Jurisdiction:**

 
 
• It is a unique feature of the Indian judiciary under Article 143, allowing the Supreme Court to provide opinions on matters referred by the President.
 
• Examples include cases related to the Berubari Union and the Ayodhya dispute.
 
• The court's opinion is purely advisory and does not have the force of a judicial decision.
 
 
 
• **Other Relevant Articles:**
 
 
• Article 131: Deals with the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in disputes between states or between the union and states.
 
• Article 136: Provides the Supreme Court discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal against any judgment or order.
 
• Article 226: Empowers High Courts to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights and other matters.
 
 
 
• **Role of the President:**
 
 
• The President acts as the constitutional head of the country and exercises powers based on provisions like Article 143.
 
• The decision to seek advice under Article 143 is often made based on significant national or legal concerns.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Article 143:**
 
 
• Article 143 ensures clarity and resolution in intricate legal and constitutional matters.
 
• It strengthens the consultative mechanism between the executive and the judiciary.

questions.question: What is the primary objective of 'Srjanam', the biomedical waste conversion system launched in 2025?

options.text: To develop a new method for incineration
To promote traditional biomedical waste disposal methods
To increase the use of landfills for biomedical waste
To reduce environmental hazards by eliminating incineration

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To reduce environmental hazards by eliminating incineration**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **'Srjanam'** is a biomedical waste conversion system launched in 2025, aimed at addressing environmental concerns arising from traditional waste disposal methods.
 
• The primary objective of the system is to **eliminate the use of incineration**, which is known to release harmful pollutants such as dioxins and furans into the environment.
 
• It focuses on converting biomedical waste into **eco-friendly byproducts** through advanced scientific techniques.
 
• The initiative is designed to **reduce landfill dependency** and promote sustainable waste management practices.
 
• By adopting innovative technology, 'Srjanam' seeks to **minimize environmental hazards** and align with global efforts to combat climate change.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Biomedical Waste:**

• Such soil is typically formed due to **arid climatic conditions** and lacks sufficient vegetation cover.
 
• The **western parts of Rajasthan**, including districts like Jaisalmer, Barmer, and Bikaner, are most affected by desertification and have extensive coverage of desert soil.

• Rajasthan is one of the Indian states most affected by desertification.

• Desert soil lacks essential nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus, which are critical for high agricultural yield.

• Rajasthan has a predominantly **arid and semi-arid climate**, with temperatures ranging from extreme heat in summers to extreme cold in winters.
 
• Annual rainfall in desert regions of Rajasthan is generally **less than 150 mm**, contributing to the formation of desert soil.

questions.question: Which of the following is the SI unit for sound intensity?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Watt per square metre (W/m²)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Sound intensity** is defined as the power per unit area carried by a sound wave.
 
• The SI unit for sound intensity is **Watt per square metre (W/m²)**, where 1 W/m² corresponds to one watt of sound power passing through an area of one square metre.
 
• Sound intensity helps quantify the loudness of sound and is widely used in acoustics and sound engineering.
 
• The threshold of human hearing is approximately **10^-12 W/m²**, which represents the faintest sound audible to a healthy human ear.
 
• Sound intensity is measured with devices such as sound level meters, which calculate the sound energy passing through a given area.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Decibel (dB):**

 
 
• Sound intensity is often expressed in decibels (dB), which is a logarithmic scale used to compare the intensity of a sound to a reference level.
 
• The formula for sound intensity in decibels is: **dB = 10 log10 (I/I0)**, where I is the intensity of the sound and I0 is the reference intensity.
 
 
 
• **Power and Area Relationship:**
 
 
• Sound intensity is derived from the ratio of sound power to the area through which the sound energy travels.
 
• Mathematically, it is expressed as **I = P/A**, where I is intensity, P is power, and A is area.
 
 
 
• **Threshold of Pain:**
 
 
• At approximately **1 W/m²**, sound intensity reaches the threshold of pain, which can cause physical discomfort or damage to the human ear.
 
 
 
• **Factors Affecting Sound Intensity:**
 
 
• Sound intensity is influenced by factors such as the distance from the sound source, the medium of propagation, and the frequency of the sound wave.
 
• As distance from the sound source increases, intensity decreases due to energy dispersion over a larger area.

questions.question: In renal physiology, which segment of the nephron is most critical for generating the osmotic gradient that concentrates urine?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Loop of Henle**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Loop of Henle** is a critical segment of the nephron responsible for generating the osmotic gradient necessary for urine concentration.
 
• It consists of two limbs: the **descending limb**, which is permeable to water, and the **ascending limb**, which is impermeable to water but actively transports sodium and chloride ions.
 
• The countercurrent multiplier system in the Loop of Henle helps establish a gradient of solutes in the renal medulla, allowing water reabsorption in later nephron segments.
 
• The concentrated interstitial fluid created by the Loop of Henle is essential for water reabsorption in the collecting ducts under the influence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
 
• This mechanism allows the kidneys to concentrate urine and conserve water, especially during dehydration.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Structure of the Nephron:**

 
 
• A nephron is the functional unit of the kidney and includes the glomerulus, proximal convoluted tubule, Loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule, and collecting duct.
 
• The Loop of Henle is located between the proximal tubule and the distal tubule.
 
 
 
• **Countercurrent Multiplier System:**
 
 
• This system involves the flow of filtrate through the Loop of Henle in opposite directions in the descending and ascending limbs.
 
• It helps create a hyperosmotic medulla, which is crucial for water reabsorption in the collecting ducts.
 
 
 
• **Osmotic Gradient:**
 
 
• The osmotic gradient is maintained by the active transport of ions in the thick ascending limb of the Loop of Henle.
 
• Urea recycling in the collecting duct also contributes to the gradient.
 
 
 
• **Role of Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH):**
 
 
• ADH increases the permeability of the collecting ducts to water, allowing water to move out of the ducts and into the hyperosmotic medulla.
 
• This process helps concentrate urine and reduce water loss.
 
 
 
• **Clinical Significance:**
 
 
• Dysfunction in the Loop of Henle can lead to conditions like **nephrogenic diabetes insipidus** or inability to concentrate urine.
 
• Diuretics like loop diuretics target the Loop of Henle to reduce water reabsorption in cases of fluid overload.

questions.question: If it is 12 noon at IST (82°30′E), what time is it approximately at 97°30′E longitude?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1:00 PM**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Indian Standard Time (IST) is based on the longitude of 82º30′E, which is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT (Greenwich Mean Time).
 
• Each degree of longitude corresponds to a time difference of 4 minutes. Moving eastward adds time, while moving westward subtracts time.
 
• The difference in longitude between 82º30′E (IST) and 97º30′E is 15 degrees.
 
• 15 degrees corresponds to a time difference of 15 × 4 = 60 minutes (1 hour).
 
• Therefore, if it is 12 noon at 82º30′E (IST), the time at 97º30′E will be 1:00 PM.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Longitude and Time Relationship**

 
 
• The Earth is divided into 360 degrees of longitude, and the rotation of the Earth takes 24 hours, meaning 15 degrees per hour.
 
• Each degree of longitude represents a time difference of 4 minutes (60 minutes ÷ 15 degrees).
 
 
 
• **Standard Meridian**
 
 
• Standard time is calculated based on a specific longitude called the standard meridian of a region.
 
• India’s standard meridian is 82º30′E, which passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh.
 
 
 
• **Time Zones**
 
 
• Time zones are regions on Earth with the same standard time, usually spaced at 15-degree intervals of longitude.
 
• Countries like India use a single time zone for the entire country, while others like the USA use multiple time zones.
 
 
 
• **Eastward vs Westward Time Calculation**
 
 
• When moving eastward, time is added to the standard time of the reference meridian.
 
• When moving westward, time is subtracted from the standard time of the reference meridian.

• The Supreme Court ruling in 'Samtola Devi vs The State Of Uttar Pradesh' (2025) clarified that eviction under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, is not mandatory in every case of neglect.
 
• The Act empowers tribunals to order eviction only if it is deemed necessary for the protection and welfare of the senior citizen involved.
 
• There is no blanket provision in the Act that mandates eviction in all cases of neglect by children or relatives.
 
• The Act also allows senior citizens to file for maintenance even after transferring their property to legal heirs.
 
• The Supreme Court emphasized that the Act's primary aim is to ensure the welfare and dignity of senior citizens, not punitive eviction measures.

• **Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007:**

 
 
• This Act was enacted to ensure financial and emotional support for senior citizens and parents.
 
• It provides a mechanism for senior citizens to claim maintenance from their children or legal heirs.
 
• The Act also includes provisions for tribunals to address disputes and ensure quick resolution.
 
 
 
• **Eviction Provisions under the Act:**
 
 
• The Act does not explicitly mandate eviction but allows tribunals to order eviction if necessary to protect senior citizens.
 
• This power is often used in cases where senior citizens face harassment, abuse, or neglect.
 
 
 
• **Supreme Court's Role:**
 
 
• The Supreme Court serves as the highest authority to interpret laws and clarify ambiguities in their implementation.
 
• In this case, the Court clarified that eviction should not be treated as mandatory in all neglect cases.
 
 
 
• **Rights of Senior Citizens:**
 
 
• Senior citizens can seek maintenance, protection, and remedies under the Act.
 
• They are also entitled to reclaim property or assets transferred under undue influence or in cases of neglect.
